newsitem.title: PERU: Christmas cheer touches even Peru hostage site.
newsitem.headline: Christmas cheer touches even Peru hostage site.

text.p: A touch of Christmas cheer eased slightly the gloomy atmosphere Tuesday outside the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima where Marxist guerrillas held more than 140 hostages at gunpoint.

As the Red Cross sent in Christmas cake to try and cheer up the hostages -- one Italian-style Paneton loaf per person -- journalists camped outside hung holiday lights on their equipment and put up a large, plastic Christmas tree.

"It's very hard to think that I'm going to spend Christmas here without my son, but that's the nature of our work," said Monica Chang, a reporter with Peruvian television Channel Two that paid for the tree. "Anyway, we plan to celebrate among ourselves with chocolate, Paneton and turkey."
In Peru, as is traditional throughout Latin America, the focal point of Christmas is a family meal the night of Dec. 24.

"I haven't even been able to do my Christmas shopping or even put up the nativity scene," explained Peruvian photographer Roberto Bernal, one of hundreds of journalists whose lenses have been focused on the residence all week.
"It looks like we're not moving from here, but we're getting organised for our own little party," said a colleague, Luis Talledo, from the local newspaper El Sol.
Cameramen on roof-top vantage points donned Christmas hats and draped decorations over the walls.

Red Cross spokesman Steve Andersen said the organisation had planned to take "something special" for the hostages on Tuesday night when they would be most missing their families. It remained to be seen if the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels would allow the gift, probably a Christmas dinner, inside.
Other Red Cross officials invited the families of hostages to write Christmas cards to take into the residence.

The only "decoration" inside the compound was a red-and-white Peruvian flag, showing a gun, a worker's hammer, and the head of Tupac Amaru -- an Indian leader who led a 18th century uprising against Spanish conquerors -- hanging provocatively from a window.

The captives -- who include about 30 high-ranking Japanese businessmen and diplomats; dozens of top Peruvian government officials; President Alberto Fujimori's brother; and some Latin American ambassadors -- were at least less crowded after Sunday's release of 225 hostages.
But they were still sleeping on the floor and suffering stifling, unhygienic conditions which have apparently caused some eye infections and diarrhoea.
The government has refused to restore phone, water or electricity services, meaning there will be no Christmas lights at the residence or calls to family members.

"I just hope the rebels treat the hostages like humans and allow them to do whatever they can to make Christmas a little bit special in these terrible circumstances," said an ambulance driver parked a block away from the residence.
Rescue workers and the 900 police officers stationed around the compound had resigned themselves to spending Christmas there and were trying to look on the bright side.

"In our work, we're used to sometimes spending Christmas away from the family," said policeman Marcos Ramirez. "This time it is going to be a good opportunity to fraternise with the Peruvian and foreign journalists, with the firemen and with my colleagues. Christmas can be celebrated anywhere."
Others were more resentful.
"This crisis has no quick solution. Things are really screwed up. We should go in now and get this over with," said police commander Hector Muguruza.

With a crack Peruvian commando unit ready to go in at President Alberto Fujimori's order, and another clandestine MRTA band reportedly at large in the capital, the Christmas period was marked with suspense and fear.

Around the country, many Peruvians said they would find it impossible to enjoy Christmas as normal knowing that the hostages were still inside. Peruvian flags put up in solidarity with the captives began to rival the number of Christmas trees.

One Peruvian bishop, Miguel Irizar from Lima's neighbouring port of Callao, urged a nationwide suspension of Christmas celebrations. "While we are not sure of resolving this problem peacefully, we cannot have parties or be frivolous," he said

The only one without a care in the world was a huge Santa Claus, whose grinning, plastic face beamed beatifically down onto the Japanese ambassador's residence from the top of a nearby 15-story building.
